claims.text: Premelting and melting of initially solid Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles are governed by cooling-induced local elemental segregation.
Slower cooling promotes segregation of lower-melting-point elements, particularly copper, to nanoparticle surfaces.
Surface copper-rich clusters act as nucleation sites for premelting.
Cooling-induced surface segregation causes earlier or more gradual surface disorder than occurs in homogeneously quenched nanoparticles.
Rapidly quenched Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles should have a predominantly homogeneous elemental distribution.
Changing the synthesis cooling rate can control the degree of elemental segregation in the target nanoparticles.
Surface-energy effects are significant for the proposed sub-10 nm particle range.
The structural mediator is the formation of localized copper-rich compositional fluctuations at nanoparticle surfaces.
Slower cooling provides sufficient atomic mobility for short-range chemical ordering.
Slower-cooling-induced atomic mobility produces surface segregation of lower-melting-point elements.
Segregated surface regions have a reduced local melting point.
The reduced local melting point of segregated regions initiates surface premelting earlier than in uniformly mixed, rapidly quenched nanoparticles.
Slower-cooled nanoparticles will begin local surface premelting at a lower overall temperature and/or exhibit a broader transition range than rapidly quenched nanoparticles.
The phase transition of the HEA nanoparticles will appear more gradual than that of a single-metal baseline particle.
Rapidly quenched baseline HEA nanoparticles will be more homogeneous and will lack significant surface segregation.
The hypothesis is limited to sub-10 nm nanoparticles in regimes where premelting is localized at surfaces rather than involving complete melting.
The proposed test compares a rapidly quenched batch with a controlled slower-cooled batch while monitoring segregation and thermal disorder in situ.
Observation of similar uniform premelting and melting behavior in both batches, together with no localized elemental segregation, would falsify the proposed segregation-controlled mechanism.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome invokes comparison with a single-metal baseline, whereas the explicitly defined baseline is a rapidly quenched Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu HEA nanoparticle. These are different controls.
